title: Growing a Neural Network in Breadth, Depth, and Time
claim: The space of possible computational structures is a lattice over resource axes, and each model occupies a distinct subset and position.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, 3D lattice cartoon plus scatter of resource-use space
description: Panel a shows a large 3D grid lattice of black, gray and light-gray nodes. It is labeled 'infinite lattice' and has three axes: breadth (horizontal), depth (vertical) and time (diagonal, receding). Panel b has two small copies of the lattice. In the top copy a blue sub-block marks a deep, narrow, fast model. In the bottom copy an orange slab marks a wide, shallow, slow model. Blue and orange text labels describe each one. Dotted arrows of matching color link the two models to blue and orange dots in a 3D scatter plot titled 'resource use'. That plot has axes for breadth used, depth used and time used, and gray dots show other model instances. The eye goes first to the big black lattice, then to the colored highlights.
caption: Growing a neural network in an infinite lattice. a The space of possible computational graphs can be pictured as an infinite lattice whose axes are resources (here breadth, depth, and time). b Each model instance occupies a finite subset of the lattice with its own resource profile, e.g., deep, narrow, and fast (blue) or wide, shallow, and slow (orange). Optimizing differentiable resource costs lets each model instance find its own position in the resource-use space (right).
abstract: Brains and AI systems alike must achieve their goals with limited space, time, energy, and data. Here we focus on space and time, defining differentiable costs for breadth (channels), depth (layers), and time (recurrent steps) in a recurrent convolutional network. We optimize these costs jointly with task error via backpropagation. Pricing each resource differently, we grow a diverse set of computational graphs through optimization. We find that breadth, depth, and time can be traded off against each other at a given level of accuracy. Networks grow with task complexity and, when allowed to adaptively allocate time per input, take more recurrent steps if inputs are occluded. The time the model spends on each image also correlates with human reaction times, despite no training on human data. Our work takes a step toward a normative account of how spatial and temporal resource costs jointly shape neural architectures in brains and machines.
